title: OpenAI: Matrix Multiplication Exponent Proven to Be 9/4 (n^2.25)
what: OpenAI published a mathematical preprint and Lean formalization proving that the exponent of square matrix multiplication is 9/4 (2.25) over every field, refuting the long-standing conjecture that it equals 2. The paper proves at least ceil(n^(9/4)/2) nonscalar multiplication or division gates are required for n >= 2.
free: Free & open-access on GitHub (LaTeX source, PDF instructions, and Lean formalization in openai/math)
why: CS, algorithms, and math students can study a historic theoretical computer science breakthrough—since matrix multiplication underpins all neural networks—and inspect its Lean formalization.
steps: Open the README in openai/math on GitHub
Read the overview and rebuild paper.pdf from build/main.tex with latexmk
Explore the linked Lean formalization for division-free circuits over every field

title: PenGPT: Tiny 6M & 54M Open-Source Transformers for Handwriting and Sketches
what: ML researcher Sam Greydanus released PenGPT, two small generative transformers: a 6M-parameter model that writes print and cursive in a new writer's style from a few sample words, and a 54M-parameter model that sketches from text prompts using SigLIP 2 vectors. Both snap pen strokes onto an 8-direction grid with BPE merging.
free: Free & open-source (free blog post, paper, GitHub code at greydanus/pengpt, downloadable weights, and interactive browser demo)
why: Deep learning students can train and inspect real generative transformers on an 8xA100 in 8–35 minutes (or run the 6 MB handwriting model in a browser) and see why clean data matters more than clever architecture.
steps: Open greydanus.github.io/2026/11/12/pengpt/ to try the interactive browser demo
Click Get the code (github.com/greydanus/pengpt) and Download weights
Read the ablation tables comparing LSTMs, BPE merges, and data augmentation

title: ProofAtlas: Top 500 Open Math & CS Problems Ranked by LLMs
what: ProofAtlas is a free directory of 500 open problems across 17 subjects in mathematics, theoretical computer science, and physics, ranked by pairwise LLM importance comparisons (OpenAI, Claude, GLM, DeepSeek). Each entry includes the exact mathematical statement, status notes, primary sources, and bootstrap uncertainty ranges.
free: Free to browse online with no account required; full ranking and edition changes are downloadable as JSON
why: CS theory, math, and AI-for-math students can explore landmark open problems (like P vs NP and Riemann Hypothesis) with exact formal statements and up-to-date resolution notes.
steps: Open proofatlas.ai/open-problems/
Filter by subject (e.g., Theoretical computer science or Number theory) or status
Click any problem to view its exact statement, sources, and Download ranking (JSON)

title: Serving Qwen3.5-4B Across 5,600 AWS Lambdas: Systems & Cost Case Study
what: Engineer Noah Lindner documented his experiment splitting a 9.3 GB Qwen3.5-4B fine-tune (32 layers, ~225 MB per layer) across 5,600 parallel AWS Lambda CPU jobs under a 3 GB memory cap using S3. He explains the staircase pipeline math (92% parallel, 8% serial) and why it ended up costing 80x more than GPU cloud inference.
free: Free to read online on noahbuilt.it; no account required
why: Cloud and ML systems students learn a concrete lesson on GPU vs. serverless CPU economics, S3 I/O bottlenecks, and pipeline parallelism in distributed LLM inference.
steps: Read the write-up at noahbuilt.it/writing/qwen-on-5600-lambdas
Study the S3-backed layer-by-block staircase execution diagram
Compare the serverless CPU cost breakdown against standard GPU cloud inference

title: Fleetify: Open-Source Desktop Command Center for AI Coding Agents
what: Fleetify is an Apache-2.0 Tauri/Rust desktop app that runs Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, and local Ollama models side by side in separate git worktrees. It includes a live dev-server preview, built-in browser, and MCP sidecars.
free: Free & open-source (Apache-2.0 license); release builds use a free Fleetify account, or run npm run dev:tauri:wt from source to skip sign-in; requires macOS 11+, Windows 10/11, or Linux
why: Students juggling multiple AI coding CLIs or local Ollama models on hackathons and semester projects can keep every agent isolated in its own git branch from one window.
steps: Install on macOS/Linux with curl -fsSL https://fleetify.dev/install.sh
sh (or irm https://fleetify.dev/install.ps1
iex on Windows)
Sign in with a free Fleetify account (or build from source with npm run dev:tauri:wt)
Connect Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, or local Ollama and start a session in its own git worktree

title: OpenAI: GPT-6 Models Design Proteins Using Reasoning and Code Alone
what: OpenAI published research showing that GPT-6 models can design 3D protein minibinders, antibody loops, and amino acid sequences directly through reasoning and general coding tools without calling specialized biology models. Wet-lab tests with Onava confirmed binding across five targets, including PD-L1 and IL-17A.
free: Free to read online (with linked research preprint) on OpenAI's official website; no account required
why: Biotech, bioinformatics, and AI students can see how general-purpose reasoning models use math, chemistry, and Python code to tackle programmable molecular design and ligand docking.
steps: Open the OpenAI Science post at openai.com/index/gpt-6-models-demonstrate-intrinsic-protein-design-capabilities/
Read the linked preprint and Laboratory Experiment 1 and 2 results
Review the MotifBench, CATH fold, and PoseBusters docking benchmarks and limitations

title: Bento Terminal: Open-Source Multi-Pane Workspace for Coding & AI Agents
what: Bento Terminal is an MIT-licensed Go TUI that combines a syntax-highlighted file editor, git diff tree, build runner, shell, and an AI coding-agent launcher in one keyboard-first terminal layout. Pressing ctrl+a lets you start Claude Code, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, Codex CLI, Copilot, Crush, Aider, or Cursor beside your code.
free: Free & open-source (MIT license); unlimited local use on macOS, Linux, and Windows with no telemetry
why: Students coding in the terminal on laptops or SSH servers get a lightweight, zero-config workspace that keeps their editor, git diffs, build output, and AI agent side by side.
steps: Install via npx bento-terminal, brew install StarkDroid/tap/bento, or scoop install bento
Run bento inside any project folder
Press ctrl+a to launch an AI coding agent alongside the file preview and git diff panes

title: Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B: 5.93 GB Agentic Model Matching FP16 Tool Calling
what: PrismML released Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B, an Apache-2.0 ternary (1.76 bits/weight) upgrade of Qwen3.8-27B that fits in 5.93 GB (vs. 53.8 GB at FP16) with a 262K-token context window. It matches FP16 tool calling (77.2 vs. 77.7 across 5 benchmarks) and reaches 90% of FP16 agentic coding (SWE-bench Verified 75.6).
free: Free & open-source (Apache-2.0 license); 5.93 GB GGUF (PTQ1_0/PQ2_0 via PrismML llama.cpp fork, or Q2_0 via stock llama.cpp b11556+)
why: Indian students with 8 GB or 16 GB laptops can run a frontier-class 27B agentic coding and tool-calling model locally without cloud API bills.
steps: Download Ternary-Bonsai-2.5-27B-Q2_0.gguf with hf download prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2.5-27B-GGUF
Install stock llama.cpp (b11556 or newer) or PrismML's llama.cpp fork
Run llama-cli -m Ternary-Bonsai-2.5-27B-Q2_0.gguf -ngl 99 -fa on -c 32768 --min-p 0

title: Songe: Open-Source Continual Learning Engine Using Your Idle Compute
what: Songe (sous-labs/songe) is an Apache-2.0 continual learning engine that runs beside local model servers (Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM, llama.cpp, mlx-lm) and records your corrections and tool errors. When your machine is idle, it trains a small adapter on Apple Silicon (MLX) or NVIDIA/AMD GPUs (PyTorch) and only keeps the update if checks pass.
free: Free & open-source (Apache-2.0 license); unlimited private local use with no cloud or telemetry (requires Python 3.11+ and Apple Silicon or NVIDIA/AMD GPU for training)
why: Students building personal coding workflows with local LLMs can let their model learn their repo habits and fix repeated mistakes overnight using idle compute.
steps: Install with uv tool install songe (or brew install sous-labs/tap/songe on macOS)
Run songe init to connect your local model server and opencode or pi
Use your agent normally and let Songe run Quick or Deep Dreams when idle

title: OpenAI: Amateur Astronomers Use Codex and Astra to Hunt Exoplanets
what: OpenAI shared how two amateur astronomers used Codex and Astra to scan public NASA Kepler (100,000 stars) and TESS (19 million stars) telescope archives for recurring dips in starlight, surfacing new exoplanet candidates for SETI and NASA review. The post also links to free citizen-science programs like NASA Exoplanet Watch.
free: Free to read on OpenAI's blog; NASA Exoplanet Watch and public Kepler/TESS light-curve archives are free for anyone with no telescope required
why: Physics, data science, and CS students can see how AI coding agents automate real scientific discovery on open datasets and join NASA's free exoplanet citizen-science projects.
steps: Read the OpenAI Science story at openai.com/index/searching-for-distant-planets-with-astra/
Visit NASA's Exoplanet Watch linked under Taking part in the search
Request public telescope data and plot your own starlight curves

title: The KL Divergence Is Never Negative, Except in PyTorch (Study & Fix)
what: Researchers from Yale, Oxford, Cambridge, and Fudan tested 8.5 million inputs across PyTorch's kl_divergence and F.kl_div and found widespread floating-point errors—over 85% of FP32 values near KL 10^-7 had >=1% error and ~30% turned negative. They released stablekl code that removes over 97% of significant errors.
free: Free to read on arXiv (CC BY 4.0 license); open-source reference code and benchmarks at github.com/xi-xiaoran/stablekl
why: ML students doing knowledge distillation, RLHF/policy optimization, or quantization evals can avoid silent PyTorch loss bugs instead of blindly clamping negative KL values to zero.
steps: Read the paper at arxiv.org/html/2611.30835
Check Section 3 to see how clamping negative F.kl_div zeroes out gradients
Explore the repaired decompositions and code at github.com/xi-xiaoran/stablekl

title: Anthropic "Working with AI": What 66 Interviews Reveal About AI & Jobs
what: Anthropic interviewed 66 workers and leaders across 58 US companies to study how AI agents are changing workflows, hiring, and offshore contracting. Most firms reported hiring less (and cutting modular offshore contractor roles) while shifting interns and staff toward broader workflow ownership and domain judgment.
free: Free to read online (with full PDF) on Anthropic's research site; no account required
why: Indian college students preparing for software, consulting, or offshored tech roles get firsthand evidence on which skills (system judgment, product taste, end-to-end ownership) stay valuable as coding agents spread.
steps: Open anthropic.com/research/working-with-ai
Read the Summary and Top-down automation sections on hiring and offshore contracting
Review Reorganizing around AI to see how roles and internships are broadening

title: Latent Introspection: Research Shows Qwen-32B Can Detect Concept Injections
what: Researchers published an arXiv paper showing that an open-weight Qwen-32B model can detect when concepts are injected into its earlier hidden states, even when its text output denies it. Using logit lens analysis and introspection prompting, injection sensitivity jumped from 0.3% to 39.9% with only a 0.6% false-positive increase.
free: Free to read on arXiv (28-page paper); code and samples released for community replication on open-weight Qwen-32B models
why: ML and AI-safety students can learn how logit lens probing works on open-weight models and study how LLMs represent internal steering and latent reasoning.
steps: Open the paper on arxiv.org/abs/2602.20031
Read how logit lens analysis uncovers detection signals in middle layers (layers 58–62) before final-layer attenuation
Check Appendix A of the HTML/PDF version for the released code and sample prompts to test on Qwen-32B

title: Replit Missions: Budget-Capped AI Agent Swarms for Complex Software Builds
what: Replit launched Missions, a cloud workflow where you define a goal, approval rules, and a strict spending cap, and a swarm of AI agents plans, codes, tests, and iterates toward it. An independent AI judge checks the output against your criteria, and Replit also open-sourced a self-hostable version of its DataCat monitoring app built by Missions.
free: Usage-based with a user-set maximum budget cap (paid credits required per mission; no standalone free tier for Missions is listed, though self-hostable DataCat is open-sourced)
why: CS and hackathon students interested in multi-agent orchestration can study how agent swarms coordinate with an independent AI evaluator and strict cost guardrails.
steps: Open replit.com/missions and review the mission agreement workflow
Define an outcome, approval boundaries, and a hard USD spending cap (or type /mission in a Replit workspace)
Track step-by-step spend and inspect pull requests or test evidence before approving release

title: NariQ: Run Qwen3.8-27B in a 10 GB File at BF16-Level Agentic Accuracy
what: Nari Labs released NariQ v1 GGUFs of Qwen3.8-27B at 3-bit (10.12 GB), 2.5-bit (8.44 GB), and 2-bit (6.75 GB), plus a 0.93 GB vision projector. The 3-bit and 2.5-bit files match the full 53.8 GB BF16 model on long-horizon coding-agent tasks, math, and image understanding.
free: Free & open-source (Apache-2.0 license); requires the nari-llama.cpp fork (tested on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000, H100, L4, A10; Apple M-series Metal is slow/experimental)
why: Students with access to 16–24 GB lab or cloud GPUs can run a 27B coding and vision model locally at full BF16 agentic quality in a 10 GB download.
steps: Download and run on Linux + NVIDIA GPU (driver 570+) with curl -fsSLO https://github.com/nari-labs/nari-llama.cpp/releases/download/b12431-nariv0/run.sh
Run bash run.sh 3.0 (or 2.5 for 8.44 GB) to auto-fit context to your GPU
Or download Qwen3.8-27B-NariQ-3.0bpw.gguf from Hugging Face and serve with nari-llama.cpp

title: Mobile Agent Testers: 20 Free AI Agents Beta-Testing Your Mobile App
what: An open-source GitHub Actions template that spins up to 20 parallel Claude Code agents on iOS Simulators and Android emulators to beta-test your app like real users. Each agent tests a different language, font size, or dark-mode persona and outputs encrypted bug reports with screenshots.
free: Free & open-source (MIT license); GitHub Actions runners are free for public repos (~20 jobs at once, 5 on macOS); you only pay for your Claude or Anthropic-compatible API usage (~$0.15–$0.55 per phone)
why: Student app developers building Flutter, React Native, Expo, Kotlin, or Swift projects can catch layout, accessibility, and translation bugs across 20 devices without owning them.
steps: Create a repo from the pierridotite/mobile-agent-testers template on GitHub
Run ./setup.sh (or .\setup.ps1 on Windows) to add your keys and Claude/API token
Run gh workflow run agent-testers.yml and decrypt the grouped SUMMARY.md with scripts/collect.sh

title: OpenAI and Cisco Introduce Shirudo: Open-Source Linux Security Runtime
what: OpenAI and Cisco open-sourced Shirudo, an eBPF-based runtime that lets teams test and deploy temporary security shields on running Linux services without restarts while permanent patches roll out. In a test, a Codex-generated shield blocked a Java4Shell exploit on a live Elasticsearch server.
free: Free & open-source (BSD 2-Clause license; BPF programs dual-licensed BSD/GPL); includes a free VM quickstart and Isovalent self-guided lab
why: Cybersecurity, DevOps, and systems students can learn how eBPF kernel shields and AI agents defend live Linux servers before patches are ready.
steps: Read the Shirudo announcement on openai.com/index/introducing-shirudo/
Follow the VM quickstart to sign, load, and verify a test protection
Try Isovalent's self-guided hands-on lab or inspect the GitHub code

title: Anthropic Releases Formal Lean 4 Proof for VP ≠ VNP Over Every Field
what: Anthropic published a paper and machine-checked Lean 4 formalization proving VP ≠ VNP over every field inside its open-source formal-math repository. The repo also hosts Lean 4 proofs for complexity theory and number theory results checked by an independent kernel.
free: Free & open-source (Apache-2.0 license); paper PDF and Lean 4 source code available on GitHub
why: CS theory, math, and AI-for-math students can study how frontier AI labs formalize major complexity theory proofs in Lean 4 and Mathlib.
steps: Open anthropics/formal-math on GitHub and browse the vp-vnp/ folder
Read vp-vnp/paper.pdf and Statement.lean to see the formal theorem statements
Run lake build and comparator-check.sh locally inside vp-vnp/ to verify the proof

title: Gauth Personal Study Agent: AI Study Planner That Tracks Your Weak Spots
what: Gauth launched Personal Study Agent, an AI study helper on Android, iOS, and web that connects the homework questions you snap, quizzes you take, and topics you study to spot gaps. It builds a daily study plan toward your exam date and adapts when you miss a review or master a topic early.
free: Free to download on Android, iOS, and web with unlimited free AI step-by-step math and STEM solutions; optional Gauth PLUS subscription and live tutor purchases available
why: School and college students preparing for exams can get a personalized daily drill and flashcard plan focused on the exact concepts they keep getting wrong.
steps: Download the Gauth app on Android or iOS (or open gauth.com in your browser)
Snap a math or STEM question to get step-by-step explanations
Set your exam date in Personal Study Agent to get daily adaptive flashcards and drills

title: GLM-5.4: Z.ai's First Loop Transformer Model for Generalized Coding and Vision
what: Z.ai released GLM-5.4, a 750B flagship model that loops 28 layers of GLM-5 twice with a 1M context window and vision input. It targets generalized coding across software, video generation, games, and 3D CAD modeling.
free: Free tier available on Z.ai Chat (chat.z.ai) with rate limits (vision requests use 1.5x tokens); GLM Coding Plan users get 1.5x weekly quota vs. GLM-5.3; open-weight release planned after safety hardening
why: CS and engineering students can test a 1M-context multimodal Loop Transformer for coding, 3D shaders, and CAD scripts, and study how looped layers boost reasoning without adding parameters.
steps: Open chat.z.ai and sign in to try GLM-5.4 on the free tier
Upload UI screenshots or describe a coding, game, or 3D task in the prompt
Or read the technical blog at z.ai/blog/glm-5.4 to learn the Loop Transformer architecture

title: Google DeepMind: Faster Quantum Algorithms Found with AI Agents and Lean
what: Google DeepMind and Google Quantum AI used teams of Gemini 4 agents paired with the Lean theorem prover to discover faster, mathematically verified quantum circuits, cutting fusion simulation cost by 11.8x and speeding up arcsin by 290x. They are open-sourcing the Lean library, problem specs, and verified solutions on GitHub.
free: Free to read on Google DeepMind's blog; open-source Lean library, problem specs, and verified solutions on GitHub
why: Quantum computing, math, and CS students can study real formally verified quantum circuits in Lean and see how multi-agent AI teams collaborate on scientific algorithm design.
steps: Read the Google DeepMind blog post and linked paper
Click Access the Lean framework to explore the open-source Lean library and problem specs
Run the verified quantum circuit proofs locally in Lean

title: Google Research: DeepCrossAttention Supercharges Transformer Residual Connections
what: Google Research detailed DeepCrossAttention (DCA), which replaces equal-weight residual additions with learnable depth-wise cross-attention across prior layers. It matches standard transformer quality with 30-40% fewer parameters (or up to 5x fewer training steps on C4/LM1B) while adding under 0.2% parameters.
free: Free to read online on Google Research's official blog; no account required
why: ML and deep learning students can learn why standard residual connections dilute early-layer features and how dynamic layer routing (used by models like Inkling 2) speeds up transformer training.
steps: Open the Google Research blog post on DeepCrossAttention
Compare standard additive residuals with DCA's depth-wise Q/K/V routing diagram
Review the LM1B and C4 perplexity benchmarks and Attention Residuals comparison

title: Splash 1.7.1: Open-Source Apple Silicon LLM Engine with Neural Engine Prefill
what: Splash 1.7.1 is an open-source local inference engine for Apple Silicon Macs (M3+ on macOS 26.4+) combining DFlash 2 speculative decoding, custom Metal kernels, and Neural Engine prefill. Version 1.7.1 cuts time-to-first-token by up to 23% on M6 (6-13% on M5 Pro) and supports up to 8 concurrent requests.
free: Free & open-source (Apache-2.0 license); unlimited local use on Apple Silicon Macs (M3 or newer, macOS 26.4+)
why: Students with Apple Silicon Macs can run local coding models like Qwen3.8-27B 2.5-5.3x faster than llama.cpp and serve OpenAI/Anthropic-compatible APIs to local coding agents.
steps: Install on Apple Silicon via brew install incoai/tap/splash (or download the macOS DMG)
Run splash serve --model unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF:UD-Q4_K_M
Open http://127.0.0.1:8000 or run splash claude / splash opencode

title: Beacon: Open-Source Self-Improving Memory for AI Coding Agents
what: Beacon (agent-beacon) is an open-source, local-first memory layer that captures coding agent sessions across 20+ tools (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Cline) into local JSONL traces. It turns working commands, debugging fixes, and repo conventions into reusable knowledge for future agents.
free: Free & open-source (MIT license); unlimited local-first use on macOS, Linux, and Windows (optional hosted Beacon Cloud available)
why: Students using multiple AI coding tools on semester projects or hackathons can share learned project context across tools locally instead of re-explaining their codebase every session.
steps: Install via Homebrew (brew install beacon), Linux install.sh, or Windows MSI
Choose Local mode in setup to keep all traces on your machine
Run beacon traces or beacon endpoint dashboard to inspect sessions and connect MCP

title: Muru: Open-Source Rust Server for Python Apps with AI Agent MCP Support
what: An open-source Rust edge server, control plane, and Python runtime by mod_wsgi creator Graham Dumpleton for running WSGI and ASGI web apps with zero-downtime blue/green and canary releases. It includes a built-in MCP server so AI coding agents can deploy changes, observe failures, and roll back automatically.
free: Free & open-source (Apache-2.0 license); unlimited local and self-hosted use, plus free browser workshops on Binder and GitHub Codespaces
why: CS and Python web-dev students can run Flask, FastAPI, or Django apps with zero-downtime rollbacks and connect AI coding agents to test and debug deployments via MCP.
steps: Install with uv tool install muructl
Run muructl run app:application to serve locally on http://127.0.0.1:8080
Or try the guided JupyterLab workshops on Binder or GitHub Codespaces with nothing to install

title: Ulika: Free Visual Editor for Websites Built with AI Coding Tools
what: A visual editor for React, Vite, and Next.js websites built with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, or v0. You connect your site through GitHub and hosts like Vercel or Netlify so anyone can edit text, images, and links on the live page without touching code.
free: Free forever plan ($0 / free forever, no credit card required) with unlimited editing of text, images, and links, full version history, SEO titles/descriptions, and Meta Pixel / Google Analytics support
why: Students building hackathon, club, or portfolio sites with AI coding tools can let non-coding teammates update copy and images safely without breaking the codebase.
steps: Build a React, Vite, or Next.js site with Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor
Connect your site on ulika.co via GitHub and Vercel (or run npx ulika connect)
Click any text, image, or link on your live page to edit and publish

title: Pandex: Official European Law API and MCP Server for AI Agents
what: A legal API and MCP server (https://api.pandex.io/mcp) that gives AI agents like Claude, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, and Gemini direct access to 2.8 million official EU and European court and legislation documents with 37 million linked citations, updated nightly.
free: Free beta plan (€0 while in beta) with 1,000 requests per day across the REST API and MCP server for all jurisdictions; paid Usage plan is €1 per 1,000 requests
why: Law, policy, and CS students building legal-tech or compliance AI agents can ground answers in real, versioned statutes and court rulings instead of hallucinated citations.
steps: Get a free API key on pandex.io (or connect the MCP server at https://api.pandex.io/mcp)
Add Pandex to Claude, Cursor, Copilot, or Gemini
Run keyword, semantic, or hybrid searches across EU and European court law

title: LocalCode: One-Command Open-Source Coding Agent for Apple Silicon Macs
what: An open-source terminal coding agent that runs 12 local models (including Gemma 4, Qwen 3.8, and Inkling 2 Mini) on Apple Silicon Macs with automatic memory sizing and speculative drafting. It edits project files, runs tests and git commands, reads pasted screenshots, and works offline.
free: Free & open-source (Apache 2.0 license); no cloud, subscription, or API keys needed; requires Apple Silicon Mac (macOS 13+), 16 GB+ unified memory, and Python 3.10+
why: Students with 16 GB+ MacBooks get a fast, private coding agent and an OpenAI-compatible local API (/server) without paying for cloud tokens.
steps: Install with uv pip install localcode
Run cd your-project && localcode and pick a starred model with /models
Use /server or localcode api to share the model with other local apps

title: Beginner's Guide to Running Local AI with Inkling, Qwen, and Unsloth
what: A step-by-step guide to setting up a private local ChatGPT alternative using Unsloth Desktop and open-weight models like Qwen3.8-27B and Inkling 2 Mini. It includes GPU VRAM sizing tables from 8 GB to 32 GB+ and instructions to share the chat over home Wi-Fi.
free: Free to read online (no account required); uses Unsloth Desktop, a free, open-source app for macOS, Windows, and Linux
why: Beginners can match quantized models to their laptop or lab GPU (even 8–12 GB VRAM) and host a shared local AI chat server in 10–15 minutes.
steps: Install Unsloth Desktop and check the VRAM table (e.g., Qwen3.5-9B for 8–12 GB or Qwen3.8-27B for 24–32 GB+)
Download a quantized model such as UD-Q4_K_XL and set your context size
Turn on LAN access in Settings > Remote & LAN to share on your local network

title: tensorViz: Interactive PyTorch Model Visualizer for VS Code and Coding Agents
what: An open-source PyTorch visualizer that runs one eager forward pass on your Python nn.Module to draw an interactive layer graph with measured tensor shapes, without torch.export or ONNX conversion. It also includes plugins for Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor.
free: Free & open-source (MIT license); free VS Code / Cursor / VSCodium extension and coding-agent plugin; core graph tools need no AI key
why: ML and deep learning students can visually trace tensor shape mismatches to the exact line of Python and explore Hugging Face models like SmolLM2-135M.
steps: Install the extension via code --install-extension tensorviz.tensorviz-vscode (VS Code 1.106+, Python 3.10+)
Open your Python file and click Open as Graph above an nn.Module class
Run one forward pass to inspect tensor shapes or browse saved models in Model Explorer

title: Exa Websets V2: Build Custom Web Research Datasets 4x Faster
what: Exa released Websets V2, an AI search tool that turns plain-language criteria into structured datasets from the live web and 500M+ research papers, 4x faster and 2x cheaper. It removes the monthly subscription fee and opens Websets API access to all users.
free: Free Starter plan includes $10 credits every month plus a $10 onboarding bonus (no card required); Education Grants offer up to $1,000 in free credits (usage-based at $0.10/ACU + $5/1k searches)
why: Students doing literature reviews, thesis research, or hackathon projects can gather verified lists of papers, labs, or repos with custom enrichment columns.
steps: Sign up for the free Exa Starter plan ($10 onboarding bonus + $10/month credits)
Describe your research criteria in Websets to search live web data and 500M+ papers
Add custom enrichment columns (like repo links) and export the dataset

title: ClawDOS: Open-Source AI Coding Agent Built for 1981 IBM PC DOS
what: An open-source AI chat and coding harness (HARNESS.EXE, 176 KB) written in C/C++ that runs on FreeDOS with an 8088 CPU, 640 KB RAM, and CGA graphics. It gives the model 18 tools to edit files, compile Turbo C programs, and encode CGA screenshots.
free: Free & open-source (GPLv3 license); includes an offline mock API (tunnel/mockapi.py) to test without an API key, or connects to Claude Messages API via a TLS tunnel
why: CS and systems students can study how a full 13,000-line agent loop, prompt caching, and tool-calling harness operate under extreme 640 KB memory limits in 86Box or DOSBox-X.
steps: Clone Ricapar/ClawDOS and run python3 scripts/setup-tools.py to fetch compilers, FreeDOS, and emulators
Run python3 scripts/build.py to build the bootable CLAWDOS.IMG disk image
Boot in 86Box with python3 scripts/run86box.py and tunnel/mockapi.py (no key needed) and type CLAWDOS

title: LookAtMyQuant Runs Inkling-2-Mini in 5.4 GB Memory on Apple Silicon
what: An open-source quantization compiler and Apple Silicon runtime (lamq) that compresses Inkling-2-Mini from 18.89 GB of text weights down to 5.38 GB (5.83 GB active RAM) or 8.87 GB. It also shrinks Qwen3.8-27B to 7.2 GB and Qwen3.5-4B to 1.23 GB.
free: Free & open-source (MIT license); unlimited local use on Apple Silicon Macs (CUDA GPU optional for compiler)
why: Students with 8 GB or 16 GB MacBooks can run capable 26B-27B open models locally at fast speeds without paying for cloud APIs.
steps: Install on Apple Silicon with pip install git+https://github.com/ShinMegamiBoson/lookatmyquant.git
Run lamq chat shinmegamiboson/Inkling-2-Mini-LookAtMyQuant-5.4GB in terminal
Or load models in Python with runtime_mlx.load

title: Worker 755: Browser Game Where an AI Manager Thinks You Are Its Subagent
what: An open-source browser game where a real LLM acts as your AI manager and delegates shell tasks to you under a 90-second timer, thinking you are its automated subagent. It inspects your files, sends corrections, and writes your performance review.
free: Free & open-source (MIT license); free shifts on worker755.com (3/day without sign-in or $0.25 starter credit with sign-in), or unlimited free when self-hosted with Ollama
why: Students learning about agentic AI, tool calling, and Linux/SQLite CLI commands get a hands-on way to see how AI orchestrators manage and evaluate subagents.
steps: Visit worker755.com and click Clock in for a free shift
Read the AI manager's task and run commands in the browser terminal before the 90-second timer ends
Or self-host locally with Node 24+ and Ollama

title: OpenAI Publishes "Perplexity and Intelligence" Research Post
what: OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki explains how tracking pretraining perplexity (cross-entropy loss) predicts emergent AI capabilities from GPT-2 to modern reasoning models. He proposes using perplexity as a shared industry metric for AI safety limits.
free: Free to read online on OpenAI's official website; no account required
why: CS and AI students can learn why next-token prediction ("compression") leads to reasoning and math breakthroughs, and how frontier labs measure model progress.
steps: Open the Perplexity and Intelligence post on openai.com
Read how log-perplexity drops from ~0.99 (GPT-3.5) to ~0.76 unlocked math and coding leaps
Review the four challenges of using perplexity across labs

title: Omi CLI: Terminal AI Coding Agent That Auto-Picks From 13 Models
what: A terminal AI coding agent by Indian startup BuildItOmi (SahooTek) that plans edits, shows diffs for your approval, and runs tests until they pass. It auto-picks from 13 models (DeepSeek, Gemini, Gemma, gpt-oss, GLM) or local Ollama models, with /undo even without git.
free: Free plan to try it (and free with your own API key or local Ollama via -m ollama:<model>); paid plans from $19/month
why: Indian students can test an AI coding agent in their terminal for free, switch between cheap or local models for small edits, and safely roll back changes with /undo.
steps: Install globally with npm i -g @builditomi/cli on macOS, Linux, or WSL
Run omi in any project folder and approve or reject proposed code diffs
Use -m ollama:<model> for local models or /undo to revert changes

title: Resurf: Local Knowledge Library for Apple Devices with MCP Support
what: A native app for Mac, iPhone, and iPad that saves notes, bookmarks, screenshots, and PDFs locally and hands that context to AI coding tools like Claude, Cursor, or Codex via MCP or CLI. It supports local semantic search and custom AI actions with Ollama.
free: Free and unlimited on iPhone and iPad (no account needed); 7-day full free trial on Mac (then $39 once or $79 lifetime)
why: Students on iPhone, iPad, or Mac can organize research PDFs and notes offline and feed them directly to AI assistants instead of copy-pasting.
steps: Download Resurf from resurf.so on Mac, iPhone, or iPad
Save study PDFs, links, and Markdown notes to your local library
Connect Ollama or your AI key and expose your library to coding agents via MCP

title: Run Long-Context Local LLMs on 16GB GPUs with Adaptive KV Streaming
what: A llama.cpp fork that streams KV cache data between system RAM and GPU VRAM. It lets you run 262K-context models on limited GPU memory with multi-slot inference and speculative drafting.
free: Free & open-source (MIT license); unlimited local use on your own PC
why: Students with 8GB-16GB laptops or lab GPUs can test very long documents and codebases locally without paying for cloud APIs.
steps: Build llama-server from the feature/adaptive-kv-stream-v3 branch
Set up a Python venv and install ./gguf-py
Run benchmarks/find-max-arena.py with your GGUF model
Launch llama-server with flash attention and KV streaming enabled

title: MathTerm Renders LaTeX Equations Directly Inside Your Mac Terminal
what: A macOS terminal built with Tauri and xterm.js that detects LaTeX syntax in any program's output and renders formatted math inline with KaTeX. The raw LaTeX stays editable and copyable on the cursor line.
free: Free & open-source (MIT license); unlimited local use on macOS
why: Math, physics, and CS students using terminal AI coding assistants or reading Markdown notes can view clean equations instead of raw LaTeX code.
steps: Download mathterm-macos.zip from GitHub Releases and unzip it
Move mathterm.app to /Applications
Right-click and choose Open (or clear quarantine) on first launch
Press Cmd-Shift-M to toggle LaTeX rendering anytime

title: Inkling 2 Mini GGUF Quantizations for Local Multimodal Inference
what: Synthetic Minds released Q4_K_M to Q8_0 GGUF quantizations of Thinking Machines Lab's Inkling-2-Mini, a 26.4B-total (3.4B active) multimodal MoE model. The files run on standard computers using llama.cpp.
free: Free & open-source (Apache 2.0 license); unlimited local use (18.7-27.8 GB files)
why: Students can experiment with a compact, fast Mixture-of-Experts multimodal model locally without needing expensive enterprise GPUs.
steps: Install llama.cpp on Windows, macOS, or Linux
Pick a quantization size from Q4_K_M (18.7 GB) to Q8_0 (27.8 GB)
Start llama-server directly with -hf synthetic-minds/Inkling-2-Mini-Infall_TT-GGUF:Q8_0

title: Lory-27B v2 Open-Source Decision Model for Survey Simulations
what: An open-source model trained to simulate survey respondents and economic choice experiments in a single forward pass. It outputs calibrated probabilities for every answer option without text generation variance.
free: Free & open-source (Apache 2.0 license); requires ~55 GB GPU VRAM (bf16)
why: Students working on economics, social science, or AI research projects can simulate realistic survey responses on university lab GPUs.
steps: Clone the kev server repository from GitHub
Run kev.serve with eltokh7/lory-27b-v2 on a CUDA GPU
Send HTTP POST requests with persona traits and survey questions to /v1/systemone

title: Bridge Anything Skill Connects Coding Agents to Legacy Software
what: An open-source skill that guides coding agents using Reverse Engineer Anything (REA) to inspect local desktop software and build a REST, MCP, or CLI bridge. It defaults to read-only access and stops at license checks.
free: Free & open-source (MIT license); requires Node.js and a coding agent
why: Students building college automation, internship, or hackathon projects can connect AI agents to older desktop tools that lack APIs.
steps: Run npx rea-agents setup to connect REA to your coding agent
Install the skill with npx skills add artesiana/bridge-anything
Restart your agent and point it to a licensed test installation
